title: Rabbi Aha (Tanna of baraitot)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman places him among the last of the Tannaim, of the generation of Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi]. In [Berakhot 13b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.13b.3) he says in the name of R' Yehuda (the reading of Tosafot and of Dikdukei Soferim is R' Ahai); and Hyman cites [Shabbat 79b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.79b.4) and [Menachot 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.32b.2) for a ruling of R’ Aha declaring [a matter] valid in the name of R' Ahi bar R' Hanina, and some say in the name of R' Yaakov bar R' Hanina (in Dikdukei Soferim: R' Ahai or Ahi).[^12] And in the Mekhilta, Mishpatim, ch. 5, he disagrees with R' Hanina bar Idi; in [Shabbat 32a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.32a.8) he disagrees with R' Elazar; in [Shabbat 127a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.127a.3) he disagrees with R' Shimon; in Gittin 30b he disagrees with Ra"bi [supplied רא״בי; compare Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov in the parallel at [Gittin 30a:19](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.30a.19)]; in [Berakhot 53b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.53b.31) there is a dispute among R' Zilai, R' Aha, and R' Zuhamai; in [Berakhot 2b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.2b.13), Kiddushin 22a in Hyman’s citation (compare [Kiddushin 22b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.22b.13)), and [Bava Batra 75b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.75b.13): 'R' Ahi, and some say R' Aha, says.' And in [Bava Batra 36b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.36b.2): 'Who is meant by “Some say”? R’ Aha.'[^13] All of these are baraitot, and so he is mentioned in the baraita in Shabbat 119a, Yoma 19a in Hyman’s citation (compare [Yoma 19b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.19b.10)), [Yevamot 121b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.121b.2), [Bava Batra 93a:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.93a.6). It is possible that what is said in [Nedarim 8b:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.8b.5), 'R' Yitzhak bar Tavla said in the name of R' Hiyya Arikha of the school of R' Aha,' refers to the Tanna R' Aha. And in the Tosefta, Shabbat end of ch. 16 and Kelim ch. 6 halakha 8: R' Aha in the name of R' Akiva. Among those who speak in his name we find, in Rosh Hashana ch. 3 halakha 9, R' Yuda Gizraya in his name, and in Pesikta Rabbati, [the chapter] 'On the Eighth Day,' followed by the supplied בב, R' Shimon ben Halafta in his name; Hyman concludes from this that he was among the last of the Tannaim.

In [Yerushalmi Ketubot 5:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Ketubot.5.11.3), R’ Aha reports that “we answered Amen after her.” Hyman calls this a scribal error and says it should read ‘and they answered’ after her, as in [Ketubot 66b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.66b.10).[^12] Hyman identifies this R’ Aha as the amora familiar from the Yerushalmi and says that he relates an incident from the time of the Temple. Hyman also cites R’ Aha in the Zohar, Shemot 17b.

The named Davidson Gittin30a baraita reads Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Ahai; the whole30b continuation does not contain that baraita. This supports an occurrence-specific comparison for רא״בי, while the supplied30b label and siglum remain visible. It does not establish printed letters, expand the siglum everywhere, merge all Aha/Ahi/Ahai occurrences or establish the proposed Nedarim identity. Hyman’s Ketubot correction and distinction between Tanna and later Amora remain his claims.

The named digital passages preserve differing forms and titles: Berakhot 13b has Rabbi Acha in Rabbi Yehudah’s name; Shabbat 79b has Rabbi Achai bar Chanina with an alternative Rabbi Yaakov beRabbi Chanina, whereas Menachot 32b has Rabbi Achai beRabbi Chanina with an alternative Rabbi Akiva beRabbi Chanina. Berakhot 53b fully writes Rav Acha beside Rabbi Zilai, Rabbi Zivai and Rabbi Zuhamai. Berakhot 2b and Bava Batra 75b have Ahai/Acha variants; the parallel at Kiddushin 22b has Assi/Acha, beside Hyman’s retained22a/Ahi wording. The cited Yoma teaching appears at19b in this digital division, beside his19a. Tosefta Kelim Kamma6:8 has R’ Acha in Rabbi Akiva’s name; Pesikta Rabbati3 has R’ Shimon ben Chalafta in R’ Ahai’s name. These readings do not identify all the bearers of the names as one person or resolve Hyman’s dating inference.

The Guggenheimer Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot5:11 paragraph twice reads וענינו, ‘we answered,’ in Rabbi Acha’s statement; William Davidson Ketubot66b has וענו, ‘they answered.’ Hyman’s emendation and his distinction between the Tanna and later amora remain his judgments. ‘Familiar from the Yerushalmi’ translates an idiom of renown, not a claim about physical gates. The Nedarim8b chain fully names Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavla and Rabbi Chiyya Arikha of the school of Rabbi Acha; Hyman’s possible identification with this Tanna remains conjectural.

The Mekhilta, Mishpatim chapter 5 reference to Chanina bar Idi, the Shabbat 119a baraita, and the Zohar, Shemot 17b reference are retained as Hyman’s supplied citations; these specific passages have not been independently verified in this review. His reported Tosafot and Dikdukei Soferim name variants also remain reports rather than a new apparatus collation. The named digital parallels support particular readings, without establishing Hyman’s printed letters, correction history, chronology, or identities.

Hyman’s printed notice (vol. I, p. 119) retains רא״בי and cites Gittin 30b. The consulted Gittin 30a baraita has Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov name the poor of Israel and Rabbi Ahi name the poor of the world. After “On the Eighth Day,” Hyman’s print has ס״ב where the supplied Hebrew has בב. The consulted Pesikta Rabbati 3 names Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta transmitting in the name of Rabbi Ahai.

In the consulted Beeri Mekhilta, Nezikin 5, Rabbi Yahai son of Rabbi Yoshiyahu gives the first statement about cursing parents by the explicit divine name. Rabbi Hanania son of Idi gives the next argument. Hyman’s names remain as supplied. In the consulted Zohar, Shemot 17b, Rabbi Aha comments on Balak’s wording about the people who left Egypt. The passage supplies the name in that local context. The precise Shabbat 119a reference remains unverified.

[Shabbat 79b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.79b.4) names R’ Ahi or R’ Yaakov son of R’ Chanina; [Menachot 32b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.32b.2) reads R’ Ahai and has R’ Akiva son of R’ Chanina as the alternate. [Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 5:11:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Ketubot.5.11.3) has R’ Aha’s first-person “we answered” twice. [Seder HaDorot 348](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=348&lang=en) also preserves that form. [Bavli Ketubot 66b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.66b.10) says “they answered” in the account of Nakdimon ben Gurion’s daughter. Hyman proposes changing the Yerushalmi’s wording on the basis of the comparison.

Gittin 30a has Rabbi Achi disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Berakhot and Bava Batra give Achi or Ahai as an alternate to Aha, while Kiddushin 22b has Assi or Aha. In the land-possession passage, Rav Chisda identifies the anonymous “Some say” as Rabbi Aha. The consulted Yoma teaching is on 19b.
